domain: Risk Assessment / Energy Policy / Technology Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the nuclear energy risk debate as a contested kernel where pro-nuclear and anti-nuclear positions read the 'acceptable risk for energy' commitment through fundamentally different risk frameworks. Pro-nuclear actors employ expected-value dominance (comparing average fatality rates and carbon benefits), while anti-nuclear actors employ catastrophic-tail dominance (emphasizing irreversible, spatially-concentrated extreme events). The measurement incommensurability is philosophical, not merely technical.

key_entities: Nuclear power plants (energy infrastructure with heavy-tailed accident severity)
Probabilistic Safety Assessments (PSAs) (risk quantification methodology systematically underestimating accident probability)
Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, Fukushima (historical accidents establishing empirical tail distribution)
Expected utility framework (decision theory with constant relative risk aversion)
Heavy-tailed probability distributions (statistical model for catastrophic events)
Public trust institutions (regulatory agencies, central government, mass media)
key_tensions: Expected-value framework vs catastrophic-tail framework (incommensurable risk metrics from identical empirical data)
Voluntary risk (driving) vs involuntary risk (nuclear accidents) (psychological acceptability asymmetry)
Technical uncertainty elimination vs social uncertainty management (epistemic limits of engineering)
Carbon reduction goals vs catastrophic accident risk (climate mitigation vs nuclear safety trade-off)
key_claims: PSAs systematically underestimate accident probability by orders of magnitude
Heavy-tailed severity implies average annual cost ~$5.5B with dispersion ~$55B
At 99.5% reactor safety, 49% probability of Chernobyl/Fukushima-scale event for global fleet
Expected utility framework is fragile under heavy-tailed distributional assumptions
Major accidents influence values and proenvironmental beliefs via psychological trauma
Uncertainties cannot be fully eliminated by technical approaches alone
Public accepts some nuclear risk if it provides clean reliable energy (trade-off acceptability)
Nuclear power viable for meeting energy demands while reducing CO2 emissions

mechanisms.description: Probabilistic Safety Assessments systematically underestimate tail risk due to model assumptions incompatible with heavy-tailed distributions

axiom_contradictions.basis: Expected-value reading treats all harms as commensurable via probability weighting (1000 deaths at 0.1% probability = 1 expected death). Catastrophic-tail reading treats spatially-concentrated irreversible harms as categorically different from diffuse harms regardless of probability weighting. No single coherent framework can simultaneously hold that catastrophic events are reducible to expected values AND that they constitute a categorically distinct harm type.

Expected-value reading places burden of proof on demonstrating harm exceeds benefits via quantified risk assessment. Precautionary reading reverses burden of proof under irreducible uncertainty, requiring proponents demonstrate safety. These are mutually exclusive epistemic stances on where default presumption lies when uncertainty cannot be eliminated.

omegas.description: If PSAs underestimate accident probability by 2-3 orders of magnitude (as empirical base rate suggests), does expected-value reading collapse into catastrophic-tail reading? The mountain of methodological fragility may reclassify expected-value as a piton of measurement choice rather than a coherent risk framework.

Absence inventory: no analysis of spatial concentration of harm (Chernobyl 2600 km² exclusion zone, Fukushima 371 km²) vs diffuse harm from fossil alternatives (global atmospheric carbon). Does spatial concentration constitute a categorically distinct harm type, or is it commensurable via expected-value weighting? This absence may indicate a fourth reading (spatial justice) not captured by the three selected.

Absence inventory: no discussion of temporal discounting in expected-value calculations. How are future catastrophic costs (nuclear waste 10,000+ year timescales) weighted against present energy benefits? Discount rate choice may determine whether precautionary reading or expected-value reading dominates, but this parameter is unexamined in source material.

Deferred axis institutional_trust_paradox: trust in regulatory agencies correlates with elevated anxiety, not reduced anxiety. This suggests catastrophic-tail concerns are not buffered by institutional legitimacy—trust may amplify rather than dampen perceived risk when the trusted authority acknowledges irreducible uncertainty. Omega: does this paradox invalidate technocratic authority grounding for expected-value reading?

If heavy-tailed distributions are empirically confirmed (average annual cost $5.5B, dispersion $55B), and expected utility framework is fragile under such distributions, does expected-value reading collapse into precautionary reading? The axiom contradiction between them may be unstable if the mathematical framework underlying expected-value is invalidated by the empirical distribution.
